runs.text:
The old editions printed their numbering in the margin, level
with the line it marked, so a reader could cite a page without
counting lines. The numbers belong to the book, not to the text:
skip them and the argument still runs.

The commentaries grew around those numbers the way ivy grows
around a fence the gardener planted elsewhere. A line of Plato
became a place, and the place outlived the commentaries that
crowded it, edition after edition.

A typesetter who feared the margin would set the number flush
with the body, where it reads as a list item or a title. A
typesetter who loved the margin set it clear of the column,
where the eye finds it without losing the line.

The second page keeps the same trade. The body runs on and the
numbers stand aside, and the reader who cites them cites the
book rather than the page the printer happened to fill.

When the editions closed, the numbering stayed. Scholars still
argue in its alphabet, and a page without the margin numbers
now looks like a page that lost its index, its argument intact
but its address gone.
